title: As Michael Kay backtracks, Yankees’ Anthony Volpe disputes report: ‘BS’
content:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — New York Yankees shortstop Anthony Volpe is one of the most polarizing players this franchise has employed in recent memory. No one on New York’s roster registers more outrage than Volpe.

It reached a new level Tuesday, when Michael Kay, YES Network’s play-by-play broadcaster, shared a report on his ESPN radio show that relied on anonymous sources and suggested Volpe refused to play second base while in the minor leagues earlier this season. Kay retracted his reporting on his show Wednesday afternoon.

“I had two people tell me, and I heard rumors,” Kay said while explaining himself in the dugout at Tropicana Field on Wednesday. “I was wrong.

“Somebody called me (on Wednesday) and said that’s not right. I made further calls, and they said no, that he had never refused to play second base. I retracted. I plan to talk to him and apologize. I feel bad. I wouldn’t want to put him in the crosshairs.”

Volpe said he learned of Kay’s report from his trainer, who told him there was a narrative out there that he was not a team player.

“It definitely caught me off guard,” Volpe said. “It’s confusing because it’s just not true. It couldn’t be further from the truth. From my perspective, that’s been very clearly communicated to Boonie and the team. I think it’s just kind of BS, honestly.

“I hope my teammates in here — I’ve played for them for three-plus years — I hope they know my character and that I’d literally do anything to help the team win. Literally anything. I think the narrative and what it tries to say about me — I feel like I am defending myself over something that literally didn’t happen.”

The Yankees initially planned for Volpe to play some second base while he was in the minor leagues on his rehab assignment and after he was optioned in May. But injuries changed the plan. José Caballero, who started the season at shortstop, injured his finger and was placed on the injured list. That caused the Yankees to recall Volpe from Triple A. Caballero eventually returned, but the injuries kept piling up for the Yankees, who were forced to capitalize on Volpe’s versatility. The result: Volpe got the bulk of playing time at shortstop, rather than Caballero.

On days Volpe did not start at shortstop, he practiced at second base during his pregame routine. He has never played any position other than shortstop in an MLB game, but that was not because he has refused to do so. Volpe said he told Yankees manager Aaron Boone he would play anywhere on the field, including catcher.

“I’d literally do whatever the team needed, and that’s the truth behind the story,” Volpe said. “That’s why the fact that’s what was said catches me off guard, because there literally was zero of that.”

Volpe, who underwent offseason surgery to repair a torn labrum in his left shoulder, said he asked the club about its expectations for him every week during his recovery. He said the team told him to prepare to play shortstop. The messaging changed two days before he was officially optioned, he said. That’s when he was told he’d play some second base in the minors.

“Even after the new message was received, I still have no problem,” Volpe said. “I want to be here, and I want to help the team win the World Series. That’s literally all I want. For anything opposite to be put out there, it’s just confusing.”

Boone said this week that he views Volpe as a shortstop, noting the team does not intend to use him at second base right now. Boone feels more comfortable moving Caballero to different positions because he has been a super utilityman in his career.

It would be helpful for the Yankees if Volpe had more versatility, but that is not currently the plan.

“He’s been our shortstop, and he got hurt and had surgery over the winter,” Boone said as to why the Yankees haven’t moved Volpe around on the field. “He’s coming back, and we really haven’t had — until Cabby walked in the door last year — a real competition-based thing there. By the way, he’s been a damn good shortstop. I hate to break it to everyone, but that still is real. Has he had his struggles? Sure. But he’s also played really well out there in some long stretches defensively.”

Volpe won the Gold Glove Award in 2023 and was a finalist in 2024. He struggled defensively last season but has bounced back this year. Among all shortstops, Volpe’s 5 outs above average in 41 games are tied for 10th.

But Volpe’s struggles, particularly offensively, have made him a lightning rod since his debut in 2023. He has not lived up to the hype that he had as a prospect. His career wRC+ is 85, well below the expectation he had as a bat-first prospect. It has become routine for Volpe to get booed at Yankee Stadium and attacked vociferously on social media.

“If you don’t perform in this market, people are going to jump you,” Kay said. “It’s just unusual, though, that a local kid — you’d think maybe he’d get more grace, but that hasn’t been the case. I definitely sense it on my radio show, and you can see it on social media.”

Boone is flabbergasted that Volpe has become a target for constant criticism. He remains unconvinced that the external discourse has negatively impacted his performance over the years.

“He handles things incredibly well,” Boone said. “I don’t think he’s affected by the different things that can be said on social. He’s just a gamer. He’s a tough kid that loves the game and plays his butt off every single day. I wish that was celebrated.”
